notes: Employer insurance deduction appeal; McCamley overruled and both collateral-benefit exceptions analysed in detail.

enrichment.short_title: Deductibility of employer-paid accident insurance from personal injury damages
key_facts: The claimant suffered a serious workplace accident in August 1998 and could not return to work before ill-health termination in March 2000.
While off work he received sick pay and £122,787.18 under the employer's group personal accident insurance policy.
The defendants admitted liability and disputed whether the insurance proceeds should be deducted from damages for loss of earnings.
A preliminary issue trial held the payments were not deductible; the Court of Appeal allowed the employers' appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a preliminary issue decision on deductibility of collateral benefits in a personal injury damages assessment.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; insurance payments of £122,787.18 are deductible from damages; McCamley v Cammell Laird should no longer be followed.
enrichment.ratio: Payments by an employer tortfeasor under a group accident insurance scheme are neither benevolent third-party gifts nor insurance monies paid by the claimant; the insurance exception requires evidence that the employee paid or contributed to the premium, which was absent here.
legal_issues: Whether employer insurance payments fall within the benevolence exception to the rule against double recovery
Whether McCamley v Cammell Laird remains good law
Whether the insurance exception applies where the employee did not pay or contribute to premiums
Whether fruits of the employee's labour can constitute indirect premium contribution

notes: French extradition after UK drug conspiracy conviction; autrefois convict and abuse arguments clearly rejected.

enrichment.short_title: Extradition to France after UK conviction for related cannabis conspiracy
key_facts: Andre Caddoux pleaded guilty in England to a long-running conspiracy to import cocaine and cannabis, including a 2.5-tonne Morocco-to-France cannabis movement.
France later sought extradition on three 1997 French drug charges arising from the same cannabis consignment.
Bow Street committed him pending the Secretary of State's decision after rejecting autrefois convict and abuse of process arguments.
Caddoux applied for habeas corpus and renewed judicial review of the committal decision.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for habeas corpus and renewed permission application for judicial review of extradition committal.
enrichment.outcome: Both applications dismissed; extradition may proceed because the French charges allege a different conspiracy from the English conviction.
enrichment.ratio: Autrefois convict under section 6(3) applies only where the same offence is charged in fact and law; a French conspiracy involving Evrard and others is not the same agreement as the wider English conspiracy, and section 11(3) does not permit this court to exercise a broad abuse-of-process jurisdiction to block return.
legal_issues: Whether section 6(3) bars extradition because of the Central Criminal Court guilty plea
Whether the French and English charges relate to the same offence
Whether extradition would be unjust or oppressive under section 11(3)
Whether deportation and extradition proceedings were incompatible
linked_authorities: Connelly v DPP [1964] AC 1254
R v Beedie [1998] QB 356
R v Governor of Brixton Prison ex parte Soblen [1963] 2 QB 243
Kashamu (No 2) [2002] QB 887

confidence.notes: Core autrefois and section 11 analysis is clear. Some deportation timing points were noted but not decisive.

notes: Second major s.3(5) Defamation Act 1996 damages assessment; awards and discount methodology fully reasoned.

enrichment.short_title: Damages assessment after accepted offers of amends in Jimmy Nail libel claims
key_facts: Jimmy Nail sued over a 2002 News of the World article and a 1998 biography, both containing sexual and professional misconduct allegations accepted as false.
Defendants made unqualified offers of amends; apologies were published and only compensation remained for assessment.
The claimant delayed suing over the book but pursued the newspaper after tabloid republication linked to Auf Wiedersehen Pet.
Eady J assessed damages at £7,500 for the book and £22,500 for the newspaper after a 50% offer-of-amends discount.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Joint assessment hearing under section 3(5) of the Defamation Act 1996 following accepted offers of amends in two related libel actions.
enrichment.outcome: Damages awarded at £7,500 for the book and £22,500 for the News of the World article; methodology for offer-of-amends discounts explained.
enrichment.ratio: Assessment under section 3(5) requires proportionate compensation with reference to personal injury comparators and a substantial discount for defendants who accept unqualified offers of amends, but unqualified acceptance binds the court to the pleaded meanings and does not permit back-door justification.
legal_issues: Correct approach to compensation under the offer of amends regime
Whether delay and failure to complain about the book should reduce damages
Aggravating and mitigating factors on a section 3(5) assessment
Whether late defendant evidence may be treated as aggravating

notes: Indecent images sentence appeal with detailed Oliver guideline practice directions.

enrichment.short_title: Sentence reduced for possession of indecent images where image levels undisclosed

statutes_considered.title: Criminal Justice and Court Services Act 2000

key_facts: A 52-year-old man of previous good character pleaded guilty to 12 counts of possessing indecent images of children, including one count covering 3,735 deleted images.
Police found over 3,700 images downloaded from commercial sites; eleven specific images showed very young children in penetrative sexual activity.
The judge sentenced him to two years' imprisonment concurrent on each count without a breakdown of the bulk images by Oliver category.
The prosecution had not provided schedules showing how many of the 3,735 images fell into each severity level.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against sentence with leave of the single judge.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; sentence quashed and replaced with nine months' imprisonment; court set out good practice for indictments in bulk image cases.
enrichment.ratio: Where thousands of indecent images are charged in a comprehensive count, the sentencing judge must be given an approximate breakdown by Oliver category levels; without that information the judge could not properly conclude the defendant possessed a large quantity of level 4 material.
legal_issues: Appropriate sentence for bulk possession of indecent images of children
Application of R v Oliver categorisation and sentencing ranges
Prosecution duties to schedule image levels in comprehensive counts
Whether a restraining order had validly been made
linked_authorities: R v Oliver [2002] EWCA Crim 2766

confidence.notes: Sentence outcome and Oliver practice guidance are explicit. Restraining order issue was noted but not finally resolved.

notes: Major school exclusion and Article 2 Protocol 1/HRA damages judgment; liability split across exclusion phases.

enrichment.short_title: Human rights damages for unlawful school exclusion denying education
key_facts: A 14-year-old pupil was excluded after a suspected arson incident and remained out of school from March 2001 to January 2002.
Fixed-term exclusions exceeded statutory limits and failed to comply with notification and governing-body review requirements.
After criminal proceedings ended, the headteacher refused reinstatement and unlawfully removed him from the roll.
Stanley Burnton J found multiple unlawful exclusions but refused damages; the Court of Appeal allowed partial appeal on later phases.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal on liability only from a High Court decision on damages for unlawful exclusion and denial of education under the Human Rights Act 1998.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; no damages for March to 6 June 2001 but remitted for damages assessment for exclusion from 7 June 2001 to 20 January 2002.
enrichment.ratio: An unlawful exclusion that shuts a enrolled pupil out of school for a significant period can deny Article 2 Protocol 1 education where no adequate substitute is provided; homework during lawful temporary exclusion may suffice, but continued exclusion after the 45-day limit without readmission is a denial even if work is offered, and section 19 does not absolve the school of primary responsibility.
legal_issues: Whether unlawful school exclusion violates Article 2 of the First Protocol
Whether headteacher and governing body are public authorities liable under section 8 HRA
Effect of LEA section 19 duty on school liability
Whether reasonable but unlawful exclusion avoids Convention breach

notes: Offering to supply drugs appeal; mens rea and withdrawal issues resolved against appellant.

enrichment.short_title: Offering to supply heroin need not be genuine or capable of fulfilment
key_facts: Neil Prior was convicted after undercover phone calls with a police officer posing as a heroin buyer.
The defence was that his statements were a bluff to fob off the caller and that any offer was later withdrawn.
Two counts related to conversations on 2 and 7 January 2003 offering future heroin supply, sometimes via an intermediary.
The trial judge ruled the offence was complete on making the offer and left the issue to the jury.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction with leave of the single judge on directions and no-case-to-answer rulings.
enrichment.ratio: An offence of offering to supply a controlled drug is committed when words amounting to an offer are spoken, regardless of genuine intent, possession, ability to supply, or later withdrawal in the same conversation; contract-law precision is not required.
legal_issues: Whether offering to supply requires intent that the offeree believe the offer genuine
Whether a later withdrawal can expunge an completed offer
Whether vague or acquiescent responses can amount to an offer
Whether the offence is one of strict liability
linked_authorities: R v Goodard [1992] Crim LR 588

confidence.notes: Legal holdings on genuineness and withdrawal follow established Court of Appeal authority and are clearly applied.

notes: Autistic adult out-of-area placement challenge; Choice of Accommodation Directions and assessment defects central.

enrichment.short_title: Quashing decision to move autistic woman from preferred out-of-area care home

statutes_considered.title: National Health Service and Community Care Act 1990
National Assistance Act 1948 (Choice of Accommodation) Directions 1992

key_facts: S, a 35-year-old autistic woman, had lived at Lorne Terrace in Sunderland since 1996 after an educational placement arranged by Leicester Council.
Leicester Council decided in 2002 and again in 2003 that she should return to a Leicester placement at Sycamore Court.
Her mother argued Lorne Terrace remained suitable and that no material change or lawful reassessment supported relocation.
The Stage III complaints panel relied partly on a mistaken NHS access premise not adequately investigated.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review challenge to Leicester City Council's November 2003 decision following use of the social services complaints procedure.
enrichment.outcome: Decision quashed; council must reconsider after proper section 47 reassessment; Article 8 challenge failed on proportionality assumptions only.
enrichment.ratio: Where preferred accommodation appears suitable in relation to needs as assessed by the authority, paragraph 3(a) of the Choice of Accommodation Directions requires it to be maintained; a decision to move without a formal reassessment after changed circumstances, and based on panel reasoning on an erroneous NHS premise, is unlawful.
legal_issues: Whether Lorne Terrace must be maintained under the Choice of Accommodation Directions
Need for formal section 47 reassessment before changing placement
Role and limits of the social services complaints procedure
Whether removal interferes with Article 8 right to respect for home

notes: Landmark preliminary issues on Council for Healthcare Professionals' power to refer GMC acquittals.

enrichment.short_title: Healthcare regulator may refer professional acquittals to the High Court

statutes_considered.title: National Health Service Reform and Health Care Professions Act 2002

key_facts: Dr Ruscillo admitted an improper sexual relationship with a patient but the GMC Professional Conduct Committee acquitted him of serious professional misconduct.
The hearing lacked full evidence of the patient's vulnerability because charges were amended and no witnesses were called.
The Council for the Regulation of Health Care Professionals sought to refer the acquittal under section 29.
A separate GMC investigation into related allegations remained ongoing.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Preliminary issues on jurisdiction before a section 29 reference by the Council for the Regulation of Health Care Professionals.
enrichment.outcome: Council has power to refer acquittals and need not wait for other investigations; merits hearing to follow.
enrichment.ratio: A final decision not to take disciplinary measures under section 29(2) includes an acquittal of serious professional misconduct, so section 29(4)(b) permits reference where the Council considers the decision should not have been made and referral is desirable to protect the public; section 26(3) bars interference only while the same case proceedings are ongoing, not because of separate investigations.
legal_issues: Whether section 29 allows reference of an acquittal of serious professional misconduct
Meaning of 'final decision not to take any disciplinary measure'
Whether ongoing GMC investigations block a section 29 reference
Interaction between section 26(3) and section 26(4)
linked_authorities: Reza v GMC [1991] 2 AC 182

confidence.notes: Both preliminary issues and statutory construction are fully reasoned. Merits of the reference were expressly not decided.

notes: Myanmar asylum appeal dismissed; IAT and adjudicator credibility findings largely aligned.

enrichment.short_title: Asylum appeal dismissed over credibility of Myanmar NLD account
key_facts: The appellant, a Myanmar citizen, claimed past NLD political activity, a five-year military sentence, and arrest en route to the Thai border in July 2001.
The adjudicator found the account formulaic and not reasonably likely to be true, treating the border incident as non-political.
The Immigration Appeal Tribunal accepted a reasonable likelihood of border arrest but as a minor non-political matter.
Post-arrival embassy protest activity was held unlikely to be known to Burmese authorities or create risk on return.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from dismissal by the Immigration Appeal Tribunal of an asylum and human rights appeal.
enrichment.ratio: Where the tribunal's more favourable finding on border arrest still characterises the incident as minor and non-political, there is no material displacement of the adjudicator's credibility conclusions or failure to assess combined risk on return with post-arrival activities.
legal_issues: Whether the tribunal erred by not reassessing risk after overturning an adjudicator finding
Credibility of claimed imprisonment and NLD political activity
Significance of post-arrival anti-government protests for risk on return
Distinction from Win on prior adverse interest in Burma
linked_authorities: Win [2002] United Kingdom IAT O7008

confidence.notes: Outcome and error-of-law ground are straightforward. Country guidance detail is limited in the judgment text.

notes: Confiscation receiver costs application; distinction between permitting and requiring payment from restrained assets.

enrichment.short_title: Receiver cannot be ordered to pay confiscation appeal costs as enforced debt
key_facts: Mr Rezvi pleaded guilty to hotel thefts and received a £214,839 confiscation order under section 71.
A receiver was appointed over his realisable property after unsuccessful appeals to the Court of Appeal and House of Lords.
Solicitors billed over £56,000 for privately funded appeal work and sought an order requiring the receiver to pay from restrained assets.
The assets were insufficient to satisfy both the solicitors' bill and the confiscation order.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for an order requiring a Part VI receiver to pay the defendant's appeal solicitors out of restrained assets.
enrichment.outcome: Order requiring payment refused in principle; court held receivership/restraint orders may permit but not compel payment of legal costs, following further submissions on possible equitable exception.
enrichment.ratio: Section 82 requires receiver powers to be exercised to satisfy the confiscation order and section 81 does not provide general machinery to enforce third-party debts against the defendant's wishes; however section 77 exceptions may permit payment of legal costs from restrained property before and after a confiscation order, as in Norris.
legal_issues: Whether a receiver may be ordered to pay appeal costs out of realisable property
Effect of sections 81 and 82 on priorities between confiscation and legal costs
Distinction between permitting and requiring payment under restraint orders
Whether Article 6 requires access to funds for confiscation appeals
